source.title: From Insight to Intervention: Interpretable Neuron Steering for Controlling Popularity Bias in Recommender Systems

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains and examines SAE neurons in recommender models, measuring their association with popularity and the effects of intervening on them. This is a different setting and measurement from toy-model superposition, and bears only on the task-specific usefulness of SAE neurons as representation units.
record.gate_note: The paper assumes that sparse SAEs encourage monosemantic neurons and uses neuron steering to mitigate recommendation popularity bias. Its fairness and ranking results are mostly outcomes of the purpose-built intervention, not tests of superposition geometry, capacity competition, or LLM feature structure. The retained rows concern SAE-neuron associations with user histories and the reported activation-manipulation analysis. The paper does not test feature completeness, stability, or canonicality.
record.test_reason: The paper assumes TopK SAE neurons are monosemantic, citing prior work, and uses them as a tool, PopSteer, to reduce popularity bias in a SASRec recommender. Its results are its own method's performance: fairness/accuracy trade-offs, ablations against Noise and RandomSelect, and checks that its selected neurons track popularity and shift Gini when steered. None of this measures whether features are superposed, why polysemanticity arises, or whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units (V5). The setting is a recommender, not an LLM, so V4 is not addressed either.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that PopSteer, SAE-based identification and steering of popularity-linked neurons, improves exposure fairness with minimal accuracy loss and gives interpretable, fine-grained control. They present this as better than re-ranking and reweighting baselines on ML-1M and BeerAdvocate, and on Yelp in the low nDCG-loss regime.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies a TopAct sparse autoencoder to recommender-model user embeddings and steers popularity-associated neurons; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition setup or measure its geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering effects vary with the dataset and with whether popularity-aligned or unpopularity-aligned neurons are reduced; the paper also reports a stronger initial change on ML-1M.

fits_no_version.finding: In SASRec user embeddings (hidden size 64), a TopK SAE (reconstruction cosine 0.98–0.998) has individual latents whose activation separates popular from unpopular synthetic profiles. Reducing them shifts item-exposure Gini in the predicted direction on three datasets. Random-neuron steering does not reproduce the effect (Table 5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents on non-language (recommender) model embeddings can isolate a task-relevant concept (item popularity) that is causally usable for steering.

record.problems: The neuron-history and manipulation results in Figures 3 and 4 are presented without numerical values in the text. The analysis uses synthetic profiles designed to be extreme, and it does not evaluate SAE feature completeness, stability, or canonicality.
record.rows_left_out: Fairness, ranking-quality, reconstruction, and baseline-comparison results are not included because they report performance of the recommender or the purpose-built steering method, not evidence about superposition or whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units. The paper also reports Table 4 embedding-distance results, but those are downstream shifts caused by the intervention rather than tests of feature canonicality.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All of it: no capacity or importance analysis.
All of it: no LLMs, and no measure of features spread across neurons. SAE reconstruction (cosine above 0.98) is on recommender embeddings only.
Completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, and canonicality of SAE features are not examined. Monosemanticity is assumed from cited work.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with a V5 'supports' label is not justified. Showing that a chosen SAE neuron correlates with a concept and steers outputs is the paper's own method validation. It is not evidence that dictionary features are complete, stable or canonical. The paper explicitly assumes monosemanticity on the basis of Bricken et al. and Gao et al. The study is a fairness/recommender paper (WWW '26).

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from limited representational capacity or features competing for dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons can arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
LLM feature distribution across neurons or recovery of LLM features with a dictionary; the study uses recommender models, not LLMs.

The study examines whether selected SAE neurons track popularity signals and whether manipulating them has downstream effects. It does not test whether the SAE features are complete, stable across conditions, or canonical units of the model.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multi-dimensional.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Selected SAE neurons in SASRec across ML-1M, BeerAdvocate, and Yelp
reader_labels.reason: The selected neurons’ activation patterns track popularity-oriented user histories, and changing their activations changes fairness in the reported direction, supporting their task-specific usefulness as interpretable intervention units (fig3-ml1m-pop, fig3-ml1m-unpop, fig3-beer-pop, fig3-beer-unpop, fig3-yelp-pop, fig3-yelp-unpop, fig4-ml1m-pop, fig4-ml1m-unpop, fig4-beer-pop, fig4-beer-unpop, fig4-yelp-pop, fig4-yelp-unpop).
